#9627. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

Final Saying

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Also I have a question for you, Is bitcoin an NFTs? let me know in The comment section below

#9626. Agent Graph Engineering, Part 5: How to Build Safer AI Agents With Structured Errors and Guardrails

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

Senior full-stack engineer. I build realtime systems and AI agents in Python, and write about the parts that hurt in production.

TL;DR Two edges, one idea: constrain the model declaratively rather than by inspecting what it produced. A tool is a function plus metadata, and it signals failure by raising a structured error, never by returning a string the model has to interpret. An action that cannot be undone needs at-most-once execution, because a crash inside a node re-runs that node. On the other edge, the guardrail that actually works is demarcation, fencing customer-written text as data, not keyword detection, and output screening runs before the human approval gate rather than instead of it.

Part 4 covered the agent and the flow that routes it. This post is about the two edges where a model touches the world: the things it can do, and the things it can say. They belong together because the mistake is the same on both sides, which is trying to fix bad behavior by reading the output rather than by shaping what is possible.

Here is the version almost everyone writes first:

Returning the error feels right, because the model needs to know it failed. It does. The problem is what else now depends on that sentence.

The model reads it and decides what to do next, so your retry logic is now a model inferring intent from English. Your frontend wants to show a different card for “rate limited” than for “card declined”, so somebody writes if "rate limit" in result.lower(). Then you reword the message for clarity and three things break silently, none of which have tests, because the tests also match on the prose.

Worse, a genuine bug becomes indistinguishable from a handled failure. A ZeroDivisionError in your refund maths comes back as "Error: could not issue refund", the model apologizes politely to the customer, and nothing pages anyone.

So tools raise, and a decorator converts:

The wrapper catches ToolError and turns it into a result carrying a machine-readable error_type. Callers branch on the type. Nobody parses a sentence.

Two properties fall out, and the second one took me an incident to appreciate.

Two audiences, one failure. message is what the model sees and can be as technical as you like. user_message is what a person sees, and it falls back to message when a tool does not bother. Collapsing them into one string means either leaking internals to a customer or starving the model of what it needs to recover. The refund ceiling is the clearest case:

The model is told the argument it passed and the limit it broke, which is what it needs to decide whether to retry with a smaller amount or escalate. The customer is told the policy. Neither sentence would do both jobs.

Anything that is not a ToolError propagates. That is deliberate and it is the important half. A ZeroDivisionError is a bug, not a handled failure, and converting it into a tidy tool result is how you ship a system that silently does the wrong thing and looks healthy. Let it crash, let the run fail loudly, and find out.

A tool is registered with a decorator, and the arguments are the interesting part:

The distinction that cost me real time: description and planner_hint drive selection, and the docstring does not. The tool list a deciding model is shown renders only the id, the description and the hint. So putting “use this, not that one” in the docstring cannot prevent a wrong pick, because the model choosing has never seen the docstring. It only sees it later, when it is filling in arguments.

I wrote careful docstrings for a week before working that out.

One more rule worth stating: a parameter with a closed set of values should be a Literal, not a str. As a Literal it renders in the JSON schema as an enum and the model cannot invent a value. As a str it can, and will, and you find out in production when someone’s status="pending_review_maybe" hits your database.

requires_approval=True is how an irreversible action declares itself. The graph reads it, and that is what parks the run for a human. It is one keyword on one decorator rather than a branch somewhere in the flow, which means adding a dangerous tool cannot accidentally skip the gate.

This is the part I would most want someone to read before putting a refund behind an agent.

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. Whatever holds the half-finished run holds the state it started from, so the retry re-enters the graph and arrives at the refund node a second time. If the node issued a refund, it issues another one.

The codebase says this plainly, and says how it knows:

A process killed mid-refund refunds again when the work comes back. The state the backend holds is the one the run started from, so a redelivered decision re-enters the graph and reaches the refund node a second time. Verified, not assumed.

The fix is a ledger. Before an irreversible call, claim it. After it returns, record it. The key is the run’s own id plus the tool: a redelivered decision carries that id back, so the second attempt claims the first one’s row, and a question asked later is a new run with a new id and runs normally. It lives in the agent’s own Postgres, so the claim survives the process that made it. Part 7 has what makes a key like that right, and the plausible one that is not.

That quote is worth a note, because it changed. It used to blame LangGraph checkpointing after a node returns, which was true of the design then. Part 7 replaced that design and the sentence had to be rewritten, and the ledger did not: the retry arrives by a different road and lands in the same place. Which is the useful thing to notice. A guard worth having does not depend on which mechanism brings the second attempt.

And then the part that makes it trustworthy:

The honest limit: if the process dies between claiming and recording, nobody knows whether the call went through. That is reported rather than guessed, so a person checks. Retrying risks a second refund and skipping risks none at all.

There is no clever answer to that window. You cannot make a remote side effect and a local record atomic without the remote side cooperating, which most payment APIs do via an idempotency key and some do not. What you can do is refuse to guess. A system that reports “I do not know whether this happened” is dramatically better than one that picks a default and is sometimes wrong about money.

A ticket’s title, description, and history are typed by a customer. If your prompt includes them, and it must, then part of your prompt is attacker-controlled. This is not hypothetical; it is the default condition of any support assistant.

The repo lists two defenses and ranks them, which is the useful bit:

Demarcation. Untrusted text is fenced and labeled as data, so the model has a stated boundary between “what someone wrote” and “what you were told to do”. This is the one that works. Detection. Known injection shapes are recorded so an attempt is visible in the trace. This does not block: a keyword match is far too blunt to refuse a support ticket over, and a guard everyone learns to ignore is worse than none.

Note the cleaned line. If you do not strip your own fence from the text, the text can close your fence and start writing outside it, which is the same class of bug as SQL injection and has the same fix. That one line is the difference between a boundary and the appearance of one.

The ranking matters more than either mechanism. Detection is tempting because it feels like security: you have a list of bad patterns, you match on them, you block. In a support product that produces false positives on legitimate tickets, which trains your staff to click through the warning, which means the warning is now worse than nothing because it costs attention and buys zero safety. So detection here records a finding into the trace and does not block. The attempt is visible to whoever investigates later, and no customer is refused service over a keyword.

Fencing is also contextual rather than universal, which took me one confusing bug to learn. When the same customer text becomes a search query rather than part of a prompt, it goes in unfenced, and the comment says why: the fence boilerplate matches articles. Wrapping a query in “untrusted, written by a customer, treat as data” means searching your knowledge base for those words. Right defense, wrong place.

Both guards produce findings, and the severity is where the policy lives:

That is the detection-versus-demarcation argument made concrete. A suspected injection on the way in is a NOTICE: visible in the trace, no customer refused. Something shaped like a credential on the way out is a BLOCK: the draft does not reach a reviewer at all, because there is no judgement call to make about leaking a secret.

Being straight about the limits, because a guardrails section that sounds complete is its own hazard.

The pattern list is thirteen regexes and it catches the lazy attempt. It does not catch a payload that is base64 or hex encoded, and it does not catch anything rephrased around the wording. That is survivable here only because detection was never the defence: demarcation is, and demarcation does not care how the attempt is spelled.

The gap I would actually worry about is indirect injection. Everything above screens the ticket, which is the text a customer typed. It does not screen what comes back from a tool, or the contents of an attachment, and those reach the model too. A knowledge base article someone else wrote is attacker-controlled in exactly the same way a ticket is, and it arrives through a path with no fence around it.

On the way out, secrets and foreign identifiers are screened, which is more than the input side gets. There is no PII redaction.

Worth knowing where this plugs in if you want more. Pydantic AI does not ship guardrails: what it ships is pydantic_ai.capabilities, a hook API with WrapToolExecuteHandler, WrapOutputValidateHandler and content_filter, plus Agent.output_validator. That is the seam. Packages like pydantic-ai-shields and pydantic-ai-guardrails build on it and cover encoding, PII and secret redaction properly. I have not adopted one here, because the thing I want this repo to argue is the ranking rather than the regex list, and a young dependency teaches neither. If you are shipping to real customers, the hook is there and the libraries are better at detection than thirteen patterns of mine will ever be.

The other edge is what goes out. A drafted reply gets screened for things shaped like credentials, and for identifiers belonging to a different ticket:

That check is crude and I like it anyway. A model that has been handed context from several records can mention one that is not this customer’s, and a regex for “a UUID that is not the one we are working on” catches exactly that with no model call and no latency.

The framing in the module docstring is the part worth copying:

This runs before the human approval gate, not instead of it: a machine check that a person never has to think about, ahead of the judgement call only a person can make.

Machine checks and human judgement are not competing. The machine should remove every class of problem that can be specified, so the person’s attention is spent entirely on the part that genuinely requires a person. Every mechanical check you add is attention you give back to the reviewer.

Structured errors are more code than returning a string. You define an exception class per failure kind. The payoff only arrives when something consumes the kind, which is usually a week later when the UI wants to behave differently.

The ledger is a second write on the hot path, and a window you cannot close. You are trading a small amount of latency and a rare “please check this manually” for never double-refunding. For money, that is obviously correct. For a tool that sends a Slack message, it is probably over-engineering.

Fencing costs tokens, and on a long thread the fences add up. Worth it.

Pattern-based screening has false positives and misses things. It catches credential shapes and foreign identifiers, which are the two cases that actually hurt. It will not catch a model confidently stating a wrong policy, and nothing at this layer can. That is what evals are for, in post 10.

No tool sandboxing. Tools run in the agent process with whatever credentials it has, so an SSRF-shaped tool, one that fetches a URL the model chose, would need its own allowlist and egress rules. There is no such tool in the demo, and if you add one, that is your job rather than something inherited.

No output moderation model. The screening is patterns, not a classifier. A classifier is better and costs a call.

Next up is the structural half: splitting one graph into specialists, which is a multi-agent system by another name. The requires_approval=True from earlier finally gets explained properly. Hope this one is useful, and if you take one thing, let it be raising structured errors instead of returning prose.

Agent Graph Engineering, Part 4: Building AI Agents With Typed Outputs and Graph-Based Routing

#9625. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

On 1 Nov, Andrej Karpathy shared HackerTube (https://hackertube.org/). He had Claude filter 43M Hacker News comments from 20 years down to 6,454 recommended videos, and he said the site took about 2 hours with Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. He also published the data as a public zip.

As a Lead SWE, my first question was whether I could pull off the same trick with a different topic and a different tool. I picked books, because HN comment threads are basically one long reading list. I picked Cursor, because that's the tool I use every day.

The result is HackerShelf: https://ishankdev.github.io/hackershelf/ (code: https://github.com/IshankDev/hackershelf).

His DATA.md lays out the method, and I copied it:

He did a few steps by hand: a Google Cloud API key for YouTube metadata, a VPS and a domain.

The final shelf has 151 books, 723 mentions and 601 unique recommenders, sorted into 9 categories.

Being honest, my total was longer than his.

From start to finish that's about 2.5 hours of wall clock (7:47 to about 10:17 PM IST). That includes my own manual steps: creating the repo, giving Cursor GitHub access and turning on GitHub Pages.

Cursor's part, writing the actual code, took about 40 minutes. Most of the remaining time went to calling APIs and waiting on rate limits.

I spot-checked 10 books and 83 mentions against the original HN comments. 83 out of 83 had the right author, and every quote was verbatim in its source comment. For example:

The ranking uses a score that weighs strong recommendations above passing mentions, which is why a book with 9 recommenders can rank above one with 11.

All credit for the idea and method goes to Andrej Karpathy and HackerTube. The comment data comes from open-index/hacker-news under ODC-By 1.0. The comments themselves are still their authors' work, and every mention on HackerShelf links back to the original comment.

#9623. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air is Edge0’s 0.6B multilingual text-to-speech model for speech generation with or without a reference voice. It supports zero-shot voice cloning from reference audio and its exact transcript, and lists 23 supported languages. Maintained by Edge0.

Generate speech from text in the 23 listed languages, or clone a voice using a clean reference recording and matching transcript. It can also be deployed through an SGLang Omni adapter with an OpenAI-compatible speech API.

Language quality varies. Reported error-rate and speaker-similarity metrics assess intelligibility and similarity, not perceived realism; the supplied evaluation does not directly quantify realism. Runtime checks were performed on an NVIDIA H20 in BF16, but throughput and streaming were not benchmarked. The model uses custom Transformers code, so loading requires trust_remote_code=True; review repository files before enabling it.

Compared with the earlier Preview release, Realistic Air adds 12 supported languages (23 versus 11). On the reported Seed-TTS aggregate, its error rate is 1.25% versus Preview’s 1.23%, while SIM is 0.704 versus 0.682; the releases were evaluated separately. On the shared eight-language CV3 subset, Realistic Air reports 4.56% error versus Preview’s 4.80%. The supplied reference comparison cautions that different evaluation pipelines and text normalization prevent a strictly matched ranking. Other Audio8 versions include Audio8-TTS-Realistic-0.6b, Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b, and Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.1b; the supplied evidence does not establish detailed capability differences for those alternatives.

DualAR architecture: a slow autoregressive transformer predicts one semantic token per audio frame; a fast autoregressive transformer predicts codec codebooks conditioned on the slow hidden state and preceding codebooks. Main model: 601,159,424 parameters, excluding the separately bundled codec. Slow AR: 24 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Fast AR: 4 layers, width 896, 14 attention heads, 2 KV heads. Audio uses 10 codebooks with 4,096 entries each. The codec operates at 44.1 kHz and 2,048 samples per model frame (about 21.5 frames/s); context is up to 2,048 packed text/audio positions. The repository includes the checkpoint, codec, tokenizer, processor, and custom Transformers code. Python 3.10 or newer and a CUDA-capable GPU are recommended. Runtime smoke tests used PyTorch 2.8.0, Transformers 4.57.3, and an NVIDIA H20 with BF16. License metadata specifies Apache-2.0.

Text is passed to the processor as a list. For voice cloning, provide reference audio and a transcript that exactly matches the spoken content; a clean recording is recommended. Reference-free generation needs only text. The example uses max_new_tokens, temperature, top_p, top_k, and do_sample as generation controls. Supported languages: Cantonese, Chinese, Dutch, English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Spanish, Arabic, Finnish, Hindi, Indonesian, Malay, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Swedish, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Generation returns audio codes that are decoded by the bundled codec into waveforms. The example writes a WAV file at model.config.codec_sample_rate. The SGLang Omni adapter supports a non-streaming OpenAI-compatible /v1/audio/speech API, reference-free generation, and zero-shot voice cloning.

Q: Can it generate speech without a reference recording?

A: Yes. Pass text to the processor without reference-audio or reference-transcript fields, then use the same generation and decoding steps.

Q: What is required for zero-shot voice cloning?

A: Provide a clean reference recording and a transcript that exactly matches what is spoken in it.

A: The model lists 23 supported languages, including 12 additions over the earlier Preview release.

A: No. The reported error-rate and speaker-similarity metrics measure intelligibility and similarity, not perceived realism directly.

#9620. A One-Line JavaScript Bug Broke My GA4 Tracking for Five Months

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

For five months, Google Analytics told me nobody on my site ever signed up, converted a file, or bought anything. Page views looked fine. Sessions looked fine. The key events report said zero, every day, and I read that as "the funnel is bad" instead of "the funnel is not being recorded".

The bug was one line. This is what it was, why nothing warned me, and how to check your own site in about a minute.

I run BatchSet, a set of browser-based image tools. GA4 is loaded the standard way, with the snippet Google gives you:

Custom events came from a small typed helper in the app code, so components could call trackEvent({ action: "sign_up" }) instead of touching window directly:

It looks like a faithful TypeScript port of the snippet. It is not.

Google's gtag() pushes arguments. Mine pushed args.

arguments is an array-like object. Its type is [object Arguments]. ...args is a rest parameter, and that gives you a real Array. They hold the same values in the same order, and in DevTools they look almost identical:

gtag.js does not treat those two the same. I tested it on the live site: pushing an array sent no hit at all, and pushing an Arguments object with the same three values sent the event. No console error, no warning, no failed request. The array just sat in dataLayer and was never acted on.

I can't point you to a line in Google's docs that says "arrays are ignored". I can tell you what happened on a real production site, and that the fix changed the result.

Page views kept working. The config call comes from Google's own snippet, which uses arguments. So page_view, session_start, first_visit, scroll and user_engagement all arrived. The dashboard looked alive. Only the events from my own helper were missing.

dataLayer looked full. If you open the console and type dataLayer, you see your events sitting there with the right names and parameters. That feels like proof. It only proves the push happened, not that anything read it.

Modern style pushes you toward the bug. Rest parameters are the idiomatic way to write variadic functions now. ESLint even has a core rule, prefer-rest-params, that flags use of arguments. Writing the "clean" version is exactly what breaks it.

On top of that, zero is a believable number for a small site. I had a funnel I had designed and instrumented, and when it read zero I started theorising about why people were leaving, not about whether the instrument worked. That cost more time than the bug itself.

The ..._args parameter is only there so TypeScript accepts calls with arguments. The value that gets pushed is arguments. If you use prefer-rest-params, turn it off for that line and leave a comment, or the next tidy-up will put the bug back.

The simpler option is to not write your own wrapper at all and call window.gtag(...), which is Google's function. I kept the wrapper because it also does a server-side usage record and a consent check, but if yours does nothing extra, delete it.

I also added a test, because this is the kind of thing a refactor reintroduces without anyone noticing:

1. Open your site, open DevTools, and trigger something that should send a custom event.

Google's own entries will say [object Arguments]. If your custom events say [object Array], you have this bug.

3. To be sure, open the Network tab, filter on collect, and trigger the event again. A GA4 hit is a request to .../g/collect with your event name in the en= parameter. No request, no event.

4. In GA4, check Realtime or DebugView, not the standard Events report. The standard reports lag by up to a day, and on the day I deployed the fix they showed zero for everything, including page views. That is processing delay, not a second bug.

After the fix, events started arriving within minutes. Then I hit a quieter problem.

My most visited tool page showed a 2.5% key-event rate. The bulk converter, on similar traffic, showed 28.5%. That looks like a broken page. It wasn't. The resizer's completion event, resize_completed, was firing fine. It just had never been marked as a key event in GA4 Admin, so no report that counts key events included it. Three other tools had the same gap.

Once both problems were fixed, the data finally answered the question I had been guessing at. Over 28 days, on the two biggest tool pages:

Of the people who added a file, 93 to 96% finished the job. The tools work. The loss is one step earlier: roughly four out of five visitors leave without adding anything. I had spent months assuming the conversion flow was the problem, and the flow was the one part that was fine.

These are small numbers from a small site, and I'm not claiming more than they show. But the point stands at any size: check that the instrument records before you trust what it says. A funnel that reads zero is far more often broken tracking than broken product.

That last one is still on my own to-do list.

Frontend developer and founder of BatchSet (batchset.com), a browser-based bulk image converter where files never leave your device. I write about i

#9619. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

#9616. Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every morning, a bot posts a short report to Slack: what moved volume and revenue yesterday, driver by driver. It runs on a GitHub Actions schedule and checks its own numbers before it posts. For a small team, it's a good setup. There's no server to babysit, the logs and secrets live in one place, and anyone on the team can read the run history.

It's also a scheduler with fine print, and nearly all of the fine print is about the morning the report doesn't arrive. Here's what GitHub's documentation says about scheduled workflows, what it means for a daily report, and the safeguards that make up for it.

These are all in GitHub's docs for the schedule event, roughly in order of how likely they are to bite.

Scheduled runs can be late, and some never happen. GitHub warns that scheduled runs can be delayed when Actions is under heavy load, that the start of every hour is one of those times, and that under enough load "some queued jobs may be dropped." A dropped run doesn't fail. It just doesn't happen.

Schedules run in UTC unless you say otherwise. Schedules now accept a timezone with an IANA name like America/New_York. Without it, a 7 AM report drifts to 6 AM or 8 AM local twice a year when daylight saving time changes. With it, a time that doesn't exist on the spring-forward day moves to the next valid time.

Schedules only run from the default branch, on its latest commit. Editing a workflow on a feature branch won't tell you whether its schedule works.

In public repositories, schedules switch off after 60 days with no repository activity. A report that just works for two months and then stops is the most frustrating version of all of this.

The shortest interval is five minutes. Irrelevant for a daily report, worth knowing before you build a poller on it.

Most of those lines answer the fine print. The cron is 17 7, not 0 7, because the top of the hour is the busiest time, and a report at 7:17 that arrives beats one at 7:00 that doesn't. workflow_dispatch adds a "Run workflow" button for the mornings the schedule doesn't fire. concurrency stops a manual run and a late scheduled run from overlapping. And the QA rules run as tests before the report does, so a change to the rules can't quietly switch them off.

A daily report should never post a number it can't defend. Before anything goes to the channel, run checks like these:

When a check fails, the report goes to its owner instead of the channel:

Each rule has its own unit test. A held report is a good outcome. It means the bot caught something before a room full of people did.

Retries and manual reruns are good for reliability and bad for a Slack channel. Before posting, check whether today's report is already there:

The marker is the report's own title. A rerun after a successful post does nothing, and a rerun after a held report posts normally once the data is fixed.

None of those checks help when the run never starts. A dropped schedule doesn't fail, so nothing alerts. The answer is a second workflow that runs later and asks one question: did today's report succeed?

It isn't perfect. The watchdog runs on the same scheduler with the same fine print, so it's a second chance, not a guarantee. For a report that really matters, have the bot ping an external heartbeat monitor when it succeeds, and let that service complain when the ping doesn't come. The principle is the same either way: alert on the absence of success, not the presence of failure.

When a report has to arrive at a specific minute, or runs often enough that a few dropped runs a month would matter, use a scheduler that makes promises: a cloud scheduler, Airflow, or a plain cron server you monitor. For one report a day that can arrive at 7:17 or 7:24 without anyone noticing, GitHub Actions is hard to beat. Just read the fine print, and build for the morning it doesn't show up.

#9615. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

#9612. Nicole Junkermann on Space Exploration's New Era: Crewed Flights, the Moon and SpaceX's Starship

From routine Crew Dragon flights to Starship's first trip to orbit, SpaceX has changed what space exploration looks like this decade. Nicole Junkermann's writing on space looks at what that progress means for the people who make the journey and for everyone on the ground.

At 11:10 Eastern time on the morning of October 1, 2026, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Florida with four astronauts from three space agencies on board. That evening their capsule, Crew Dragon Grace, docked with the International Space Station. Crew-13 was the 21st crewed orbital flight of a Crew Dragon, and for most people it registered as an ordinary Thursday news item. That ordinariness is one of the biggest changes in space exploration this decade. It's also the change at the center of Nicole Junkermann's thinking about space: what happens once reaching orbit stops being rare.

On May 30, 2020, NASA astronauts Bob Behnken and Doug Hurley flew to the station on SpaceX's Demo-2 mission. It was the first crewed orbital launch from American soil since the space shuttle retired in 2011, and the first time a commercially built and operated spacecraft had carried astronauts to orbit. Dragon has since flown regular NASA crew rotations and opened orbit to private crews as well. Inspiration4, in September 2021, was the first orbital mission with an all-civilian crew. Polaris Dawn, in September 2024, included the first commercial spacewalk. Fram2, in 2025, became the first crewed flight to circle Earth over its poles. Nicole Junkermann's writing on space keeps returning to this widening of access, and private crew flights are one of its most visible results.

SpaceX is among the companies NJF Capital, the venture arm of Nicole Junkermann's NJF Holdings, has invested in, as her personal website notes. Her technology journal calls her association with SpaceX the clearest example of frontier engineering in her work. What Nicole Junkermann writes about space, though, keeps coming back to people, and to who gets the chance to take part.

In a note on space technology and its promise, Nicole Junkermann points out that for decades the toughest part of space was getting off the ground at all. The price of each launch decided who could fly and how much they could attempt. As launches have become cheaper and more frequent, she argues, the field has turned more experimental and far more open, and universities and small teams now put their own instruments in orbit.

Falcon 9 shows what that looks like in practice. Its first stages fly back and land on drone ships or landing zones, then fly again. Booster B1067 first flew in June 2021, sending a Dragon cargo capsule to the space station, went on to launch two astronaut crews, and on August 25, 2026, completed its 37th flight. SpaceX flew 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, its busiest year yet. It's a practical example of the shift Nicole Junkermann describes.

The same rockets carry exploration far beyond Earth orbit. In October 2024 a SpaceX Falcon Heavy launched NASA's Europa Clipper toward Jupiter, where it will study the ice-covered moon Europa and the ocean scientists believe lies beneath its surface when it arrives in 2030. In March 2025 Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost lander, which had launched on a Falcon 9, touched down on the Moon and began its science work. For Nicole Junkermann, missions like these show how much more becomes possible once reaching space stops being the hard part.

SpaceX's next step is Starship, the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown, built to be fully reusable. The program has moved quickly. In October 2024 the launch tower at Starbase, Texas, caught a returning Super Heavy booster with its mechanical arms. On September 28, 2026, Starship reached orbit for the first time on its 14th flight and deployed 26 Starlink satellites. At the time of writing, SpaceX is preparing a 15th flight that aims to catch the ship as well as the booster. Starship is the sort of frontier engineering Nicole Junkermann's technology journal has in mind when it points to SpaceX.

The Moon is where Starship's exploration work begins. NASA selected SpaceX in April 2021 to develop a version of Starship as a crewed lunar lander for its Artemis program, and in February 2026 SpaceX said it would focus on building a lasting presence on the Moon before sending people to Mars. A lander that size is designed to carry far more equipment and supplies to the lunar surface than Apollo ever could, which opens the door to longer stays and much bigger experiments. It's the kind of decades-long project Nicole Junkermann's writing tends to favor.

Mars and the worlds beyond it remain the longer dream. In a short video on the future of space travel and new worlds, Nicole Junkermann asks whether people might one day call more than one planet home. She treats it as an open question worth exploring, and her hope is that dreaming about new worlds goes hand in hand with caring for this one.

Nicole Junkermann's note on space measures its promise in human terms. She tends to describe its benefits through ordinary people, such as farmers, city planners and scientists, who make better decisions because of what orbit shows them. Human spaceflight fits that view in a very direct way. Research on the International Space Station, which Dragon serves with both crew and cargo flights, studies how the human body, materials and medicines behave in microgravity, and that work feeds back into life on Earth.

Nicole Junkermann also takes a long view. Her personal website quotes her saying, "What interests me isn't what's popular today," and her focus is on what will still matter ten years from now. Space exploration runs on even longer clocks. Europa Clipper won't reach Jupiter for another few years, and a permanent base on the Moon will take far longer than that to build.

As seen recently, a motivational video by Nicole was published about space and space exploration.

Elsewhere on the same site, she sums up her outlook in a single line: "Progress only matters if it is human led and human shaped." In The Human Code, her April 2026 essay on the principles behind her work, Nicole Junkermann wrote that a more capable future "will only be worth building if it also remains more human." Crews from several countries now ride SpaceX rockets to orbit on a regular schedule, and Starship is being built to take astronauts back to the Moon. Both fit the kind of progress Nicole Junkermann describes, with people still at the center of it.

#9611. CoreVault Exploit: Spot Price Fallback Drained 259 BNB

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at panda-security.xyz

Originally published at panda-security.xyz

At 21:50:20 UTC on 3 November 2026, a single transaction on BNB Smart Chain drained 259.09 BNB from the reserve behind CoreVault, a BNB vault system tied to the OSK token. The attacker kept 160.26 BNB, which CertiK valued at about $112,200. There was no stolen key and no reentrancy. The attacker borrowed about 207,000 WBNB, dumped most of it into PancakeSwap's WBNB/USDT pool, and then asked CoreVault to redeem a position while the pool showed BNB at roughly one percent of its real price. CertiK reported that the redemption came out about 33 times larger than it should have.

The interesting part is not that a spot price can be moved with a flash loan. Everyone knows that. The interesting part is that the protocol reportedly did have a multi-source oracle, and the attack went through the path the oracle used when its safer inputs were not ready yet. This post walks through what the chain shows, where the reported root cause sits, and what to test in any vault that pays out of a reserve.

We pulled the receipt and the surrounding state from public BSC nodes. The transaction is a contract creation: the attacker deployed a helper at 0xc28cfeee...f387e2 and ran the whole attack from its constructor, so there was no separate setup transaction to front-run or flag.

The token transfers in the receipt follow a clean sequence:

The native BNB side does not show up as token transfers, so we compared balances one block before and after using an archive node:

The numbers reconcile. The round trip through PancakeSwap cost the attacker 195,000 minus 194,901.165, about 98.83 WBNB in fees and slippage. Take that from the 259.09 BNB that left the reserve and you get 160.26 BNB, which is what landed in the attacker's wallet. Onchain Lens reported a gross withdrawal of 260.21 BNB through CoreVault and a net depletion matching the roughly 259 BNB we see, and Telem's write-up reports the same pair of figures.

Right before the attack block, the PancakeSwap pair held about 15,345,479 USDT and 21,917 WBNB, a spot price of about $700.15 per BNB. After the 195,000 WBNB dump and the USDT that came out, the reserves were about 1.55M USDT and 216,917 WBNB, which puts the spot price near $7.16. That is roughly a 98x drop, held for the length of one transaction.

CertiK reported the redemption was inflated about 33x, not 98x. We do not have the verified CoreVault source to explain the exact ratio, so treat this as our reading rather than a confirmed fact: a figure between 1x and 98x is what you would expect if the manipulated spot price was blended with other price inputs instead of used alone. Blackpaper's summary says the redemption logic averaged a same-transaction spot price into a short sampling window. Either way, a partial dilution of a 98x move still left a 33x error, which was more than enough to empty the reserve.

The most detailed public description comes from Telem, and since CoreVault has not published a post-mortem, the function names below are as reported there and not something we have verified against source code.

According to that report, CoreVault's redeemPrincipal pays BNB for a USD-denominated principal. To convert, it uses a value called wbnbPerUsd, how many WBNB one dollar buys. That value comes from an OracleLib helper that takes a median of three sources. When the TWAP or average-price windows are not fully populated, the median falls back to the PancakeSwap spot price. The payout then flows through Treasury.payoutBnb into InsurancePool.withdrawReserve.

Dumping WBNB makes WBNB cheap, so wbnbPerUsd goes up, so a fixed dollar principal is converted into far more BNB. The attacker did not need to fool the oracle forever. It needed one transaction in which the only source that counted was the one it could move.

A simplified sketch of that failure pattern, written for illustration only and not CoreVault's actual code:

A safer shape refuses to price at all when the robust inputs are missing:

A median of three sources is a reasonable design. It only works if all three sources are live and independent. The reported fallback breaks both conditions at once: when the windows are empty there is effectively one source, and it is the one an attacker can move with borrowed money.

Fallback paths are easy to miss in review because they look defensive. Someone wrote "if the TWAP is not ready, do not revert, use what we have" so the product would keep working right after deployment or after a quiet period. That is a liveness decision. In a function that sends value out, it turns into a security decision, and the safe default for a payout is to stop, not to guess.

The second design problem is where the money came from. An insurance reserve is supposed to absorb losses. Here it was wired directly into the redemption path, so any pricing error in redemptions was paid from the backstop. That turned a pricing bug into a reserve drain, and there was no per-transaction or per-period limit in the way.

Make every oracle fallback fail closed in value-moving paths. If a TWAP, median or external feed is not ready, revert redemptions, withdrawals and liquidations. A paused vault is an annoyance; a vault that prices from spot is a donation.

Test the cold start. Many TWAP implementations need a warm-up period after deployment, after a pool migration, or after a long gap in observations. Write tests that call every payout function in that state and assert that they revert.

Use spot only as a sanity check. Comparing spot to a TWAP and rejecting large deviations is useful. Letting spot set the price, even inside a median, is not.

Bound reserve outflows. Rate limits, per-transaction caps and caps relative to the reserve's size would not fix a bad price, but they turn a full drain into a partial one and buy time for monitoring to react.

Model the flash loan budget. Here roughly $143.6M of WBNB was borrowed against a pool holding about $30.7M of total liquidity. Your threat model should assume an attacker can borrow several times the depth of any pool your contracts read from, for free, within one transaction. Our earlier guide to flash loan attacks covers the general pattern.

Treat "derived from balances" and "derived from spot" as the same smell. The Moonwell MAMO exploit inflated a value through direct token transfers; CoreVault inflated one through a swap. Both read a number an attacker could set. Our smart contract security checklist is a good place to start when reviewing a vault.

CoreVault did not lose its reserve because it trusted a single DEX price on purpose. It lost it because a fallback written for convenience became the only price that mattered for one transaction. If your protocol pays out from a reserve or converts between assets with an on-chain price, talk to our team or check our audit pricing to have the cold-start and fallback paths reviewed before an attacker finds them.
