#9608. Brava Raises $15M to Address the Blind Spots in AI-Powered Cybersecurity

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Tech analyst and reporter covering startups, public tech companies, and executives. Associate Editor at The San Francisco Tribune.

Cybersecurity companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to accelerate security operations. AI agents can investigate alerts, analyze suspicious activity, and help security teams make decisions faster. But there is a problem that more automation cannot solve on its own: security systems must first collect the evidence needed to identify an attack.

Brava Security is entering the market with a technology designed to address that gap. In a press release shared directly with this writer, the company announced that it had emerged from stealth with $15 million in funding led by F2 Venture Capital and Pitango VC. Its multi-agent AI platform tests attack techniques and evaluates the telemetry they produce to identify gaps in security visibility.

The goal is to establish whether an enterprise's existing security infrastructure can recognize specific attack techniques, identify where detection capabilities fall short, and help fix those weaknesses. Rather than requiring companies to replace their existing tools, Brava works with the infrastructure security teams already have in place.

“Everyone is racing to put AI in charge of the SOC. You can't automate a decision based on evidence no one ever proved,” said Idan Basre, co-founder and CEO of Brava Security, who encountered the problem firsthand while leading product management for Microsoft Defender. “We're solving the problem that comes before AI can make the right decision: making sure the security infrastructure actually sees the threats it's supposed to detect.”

Modern enterprise environments are becoming increasingly complex. Companies are deploying more cloud services, AI applications, and AI-assisted development tools, creating additional sources of security telemetry that need to be collected, processed, and monitored.

However, having more data does not necessarily mean having better security visibility. Critical logs may never be collected, telemetry pipelines can silently break, and detection rules may fail to identify the attacks they were designed to catch. The MITRE ATT&CK framework's data components illustrate how specific sources of security evidence relate to detecting attacker techniques.

These weaknesses create a significant challenge for security operations centers (SOCs). An AI agent might be capable of investigating an alert in seconds, but its capabilities are limited when the underlying security infrastructure never generates an alert in the first place.

Brava is built around this distinction. Instead of focusing exclusively on analyzing the alerts that security systems produce, its technology examines whether those systems would recognize an attack at all.

Brava's platform focuses on modeling attacker behavior and understanding how different attack techniques would appear across an organization's specific environment and log sources.

Its Security Operations platform determines what an attack should look like, evaluates whether existing defenses would detect it, and identifies the telemetry and detection gaps that could leave an organization exposed. It can then rewrite SIEM detections and address data feeds that are blind to the tested activity, while also investigating alongside security teams.

The approach centers on understanding the relationship between attacker behavior and the evidence available to security tools.

“The hard part of security was never writing detections. It’s knowing exactly what an attack will look like in a specific environment, across all of its log sources, before it ever happens. That’s the problem our models were built to solve,” said Itay Gabbay, co-founder and CTO of Brava Security.

By testing attack techniques and evaluating the resulting telemetry, Brava aims to give security teams a way to evaluate their detection capabilities without relying solely on assumptions about how their infrastructure performs.

According to Brava, the company has already signed Fortune 100 companies across the retail, energy, and hospitality sectors. Its customer base also includes Cushman & Wakefield and WELL Health, one of Canada's largest healthcare companies.

The company says its platform delivers its first insights within 10–15 minutes of onboarding, allowing security teams to begin evaluating findings without going through a lengthy deployment process.

Integration with existing security infrastructure is another part of its approach. Brava supports Splunk, Google SecOps, CrowdStrike, and more than 70 other sources and destinations.

For Cushman & Wakefield, the platform is designed to help security personnel bring evidence together and make decisions without spending unnecessary time searching across systems.

“Our SecOps journey is about applying AI where it makes our people more effective, and Brava sits at the center of that. It investigates alongside our team, bringing evidence together so decisions rest on facts rather than on searching,” said Erik Hart, CISO at Cushman & Wakefield.

The $15 million seed round was led by Pitango and F2 Venture Capital, with participation from angel investors, including executives from Anthropic, Microsoft, and Check Point, according to Brava.

According to the company's account of its founders' backgrounds, Basre brings ten years of experience in Unit 8200, where he worked as a threat researcher, followed by product management leadership at Microsoft Defender. Gabbay spent seven years in the IDF building core AI systems, including work on a joint DARPA-Israeli research program. Their backgrounds and leadership roles are also outlined on Brava's website.

Brava says it has approximately 20 employees, combining AI researchers and security researchers. Its R&D operations are based in Israel, while its commercial team is expanding across the United States.

According to the company, the funding will support further technology development and commercial expansion across North America, with financial services and government among the additional markets it is preparing to pursue.

As enterprises continue exploring AI-driven security operations, Brava is making the case that automation needs a dependable foundation. Its approach puts the ability to prove what security systems can actually detect at the center of that effort.

#9605. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9602. Why does my challah have stretch marks?: How to stop your challah from tearing.

Recently, our Community Development Coordinator Kat Mayerovitch shared a very important update from the King Arthur Baking subreddit: a surprising amount of people were wondering why their challah has “stretch marks.”

If you’re not one of those people and don’t know exactly what that means, you may still be familiar with the problem: Sometimes, challah loaves come out of the oven with stretches or tears along the braided strands. It doesn’t affect the quality of the bread, but it does affect the appearance.

To address this issue, I asked our Baking School Curriculum Developer Jack Tissiere for their thoughts on this problem, and they identified two potential causes.

Challah dough rises twice: Once after it’s mixed (known as bulk fermentation) and a second time after the loaf is shaped or braided. Cutting short that second rise can lead to a challah that develops tears as it bakes. As Jack explains, “When we underproof our challah loaves (in other words, don't give them enough time to rise), the bread is still super active and energetic. When it hits the heat of the oven it expands energetically, and that sudden burst of volume before the dough sets can cause the bread to stretch or rip.”

How to fix: Give your braided challah loaf a little more time to rise before baking. Push the proof until the loaf is puffy and marshmallow-y; when you press it with a floured finger, the indent should slowly fill in, which is a sign that it’s ready to be baked. Sometimes, depending on the temperature of both your dough and your environment, this can take longer than the recipe says; trust your instincts rather than relying on the clock. If you fully proof the bread, when you put the loaf into the oven it’s less energetic, which means there isn’t as much oven spring (and subsequent tearing) while baking.

The other reason your challah may have stretch marks is because the loaves are shaped or braided too tightly. As Jack explains “When loaves are braided very tightly, they don’t have a lot of room to grow during the rising and baking process, causing stretches or tears as they expand.”

How to fix: Give your challah dough some slack when shaping: Braid loosely, allowing extra space for the dough to expand as it undergoes its final proof before baking. And for a pretty, even braid, start braiding from the middle; this video shows you how.

Ready to tackle your next braided loaf? Check out our Braided Challah recipe from The Big Book of Bread.

#9598. M6 Mac mini vs GitHub's hosted macOS runner: an Xcode build benchmark

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at macrun.dev

We wanted a real number for one question. How much faster is a dedicated M6 Mac mini than GitHub's standard hosted macOS runner, on a real iOS app? So we built the open-source Wikipedia iOS app on both, with the same Xcode and the same script, three times each.

This post replaces our earlier M4 benchmark post. Every number here comes from runs made on September 24, 2026.

The M6 was about twice as fast at compiling. The package download was close, because both machines pull the same packages from GitHub over fast connections. Every step succeeded on both machines in every run.

The table compares the machines step by step. A real CI job is different on each. A hosted runner starts every job empty. It has to download packages, build from clean, and then test. A dedicated Mac keeps its build folder, so after a small change it only rebuilds what changed.

Hosted: download, clean build, tests. M6 warm: incremental build, tests.

That is the gap your team feels. A job that took four and a half minutes finishes in under thirty seconds. On a busy day of pushes, the saved minutes add up to hours.

The same job costs money on a hosted runner. GitHub rounds each job up to the minute, so 269 seconds bills as 5 minutes. At $0.062 a minute that is about 31 cents a job. On a dedicated Mac it costs nothing extra. Our cost calculator turns your own job count into a monthly figure.

The hardware details come from the machines themselves. Each run printed its chip, core count and memory before building. GitHub also sells larger macOS runners at higher per-minute prices. We tested the standard one because it is what most teams use.

We ran the app's package tests, not its main test target. The main target needs signed app-group entitlements, and an unsigned CI build does not have them. Its test host kept relaunching on both machines, so it was no fair measure.

The incremental build touched one small file. Most of its 10 seconds is Xcode planning the build, which is why it matches the no-op build. A change to a widely used file would take longer on both machines.

The two machines ran different macOS versions, because each ran what its owner ships today. A hosted job can also cache Swift packages with actions/cache. That would cut the download step. It would not remove the clean build, which is most of the time.

We sell the M6 runner, so weigh our numbers with that in mind. The method above is complete enough to rerun on your own project, which is the only benchmark that really matters to you.

This guide first appeared on macrun.dev. Full disclosure, I run MacRun, which rents dedicated Mac minis for builds and coding agents.

#9595. Organic Search Is Shrinking, While Email Builds a More Durable Audience

Posted on Nov 4 • Originally published at blog.geosearchleads.com

Organic discovery is becoming a less dependable single source of website visits in the data examined by Search Engine Land. At the same time, email is growing in both absolute visits and year-over-year performance, giving publishers, brands, and ecommerce sites a stronger reason to invest in audiences they can reach without relying entirely on a search results page.

In Kevin Indig's Search Engine Land analysis of Similarweb data, email visits rose from January through August 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. The analysis also found that direct and organic traffic declined over a longer two-year comparison. The evidence does not mean search has stopped mattering. It does suggest that visibility in search and AI-generated answers should increasingly support a broader audience-development model rather than stand alone.

The analysis covered roughly 1,896 to 1,897 domains, depending on the comparison. It is therefore an observed sample, not a measure of every site or all web traffic.

For January through August 2026 versus the same months in 2025, email visits increased 16.3% in the United States and 17.0% in France. Paid search also grew in the reported data, by 20.8% in the U.S. and 20.3% in France, although those figures require important attribution context.

Email was already larger than paid search in total visits in both markets examined:

Direct remained the largest channel in the analysis, but it was shrinking. Direct visits were down 2.7% year over year in the U.S. and 3.1% in France for January through August. From August 2024 to August 2026, direct visits declined 3.4% in the U.S. and 5.3% in France. Organic visits fell more sharply over that latter period: 13.2% in the U.S. and 23.4% in France.

These are not proof that every website is losing organic traffic or that email will outperform every other channel. They are a useful directional signal from the domains studied, particularly for teams whose acquisition plans still assume organic traffic will be the primary scalable source of returning attention.

One of the most valuable parts of the analysis is its warning about routing and attribution. Paid-search estimates can change depending on how visits through Google's googleadservices.com ad-tracking domain are categorized.

When that domain was included, reported paid-search growth was 13.5% in the U.S. and 10.7% in France. When it was excluded, paid-search growth rose to 21.0% in the U.S. and 15.2% in France. In those comparisons, email growth was reported at 20.5% in the U.S. and 17.6% in France.

The discrepancy is a reminder that channel labels are not always clean descriptions of user behavior. Redirects, tracking domains, analytics configuration, consent choices, apps, and users moving between channels can all influence what is credited to organic, paid, direct, referral, or email.

For marketers, the practical lesson is not to disregard channel reports. It is to avoid treating a single channel line item as a complete causal explanation. Compare analytics platforms and tagging rules, document changes in tracking, and evaluate acquisition alongside downstream engagement and repeat visits.

Organic search, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT Search, and other answer engines can still introduce people to a brand. But discovery is different from a durable audience relationship. A citation, ranking, or mention may generate awareness without creating a reliable path back to the site.

That makes first-party audience capture more strategically important. A useful visitor journey has two connected stages:

Direct traffic deserves similar attention, even though it declined in the reported data. Direct is a mixed category, not a pure measure of brand loyalty. It can include untagged campaigns and other traffic that analytics cannot classify. Still, rising repeat visits, bookmarked access, and branded return behavior are generally useful indicators that a site is building recognition beyond one-time search clicks.

The appropriate response is diversification, not abandoning SEO or treating email as a replacement for search. Search content can create the demand that makes subscriptions and repeat visits possible. The goal is to make the channels reinforce each other.

Start by reviewing which high-value organic landing pages attract new visitors but fail to create a next step. Add relevant, low-friction subscription opportunities that match the page's topic or user need. A newsletter about the subject, a product-update list, or a recurring research digest can be more useful than a generic sign-up request.

Next, separate discovery metrics from relationship metrics. Track organic entrances, AI referral traffic where it is identifiable, email-driven sessions, returning users, branded search interest, and conversions. Do not assume a fall in last-click organic traffic means search content has no role in subsequent email sign-ups or direct returns.

Finally, audit attribution before changing budgets. The googleadservices.com finding illustrates how much channel interpretation can depend on classification. Maintain consistent UTM conventions, review redirect behavior, and annotate major tracking or consent changes when comparing periods.

If AI search reduces clicks for some informational queries, this approach becomes even more relevant. The content that earns visibility should also demonstrate enough expertise and usefulness that the people who do click choose to establish a direct relationship.

GEO Search Leads can help teams turn AI-search visibility into a more deliberate website strategy by assessing GEO readiness and surfacing optimization opportunities in content that supports discovery. If you want a clearer starting point for improving how your site is understood across generative search experiences, create a GEO Search Leads account.

Does this analysis show that organic search is declining for every website?

No. The analysis reports trends across a sample of roughly 1,896 to 1,897 domains in the U.S. and France. Performance can differ significantly by site, market, content type, and measurement setup.

Why did paid-search growth change when googleadservices.com was included or excluded?

Google's ad-tracking domain can affect how visits are routed and categorized in traffic data. The analysis found materially different paid-search growth rates under the two treatments, showing that attribution rules affect interpretation.

Is direct traffic a reliable measure of brand loyalty?

Not by itself. Direct traffic can include bookmarked visits and people intentionally returning to a brand, but it can also include traffic that analytics could not attribute to another source. It is best evaluated alongside branded search, email engagement, and returning-user behavior.

Should businesses replace SEO with email marketing?

No. The data supports diversifying acquisition and building owned audience relationships, not replacing search. SEO and GEO can support discovery, while email provides a way to maintain contact with interested visitors.

The Similarweb findings point to a practical shift in priorities: organic visibility remains valuable, but it is less safe as the sole foundation for audience growth. Sites that connect search and AI discovery to permission-based email relationships, repeat visits, and disciplined attribution will be better positioned to understand and reduce their dependence on any one traffic source.

#9594. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9590. The Sandbox Fights Back: Joe Security Launches Adaptive Detonation

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

Reinach, Switzerland, November 4th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--Joe Security's Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run.

Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions. These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments.

Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity.

The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies. By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden.

For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations.

Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic, the free community version.

Read the Adaptive Detonation blog post for technical details, malware case studies, and original and follow-up analysis reports.

Joe Security is a privately owned Swiss software company founded in 2011 and headquartered in Reinach, Switzerland. It develops malware and phishing analysis technology, combining dynamic analysis, agentic reverse engineering and dedicated analyst lab environments.

#9587. Bitbase Launches ORIGIN, Distributing 1M Points Every week

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

Panama City, November 4, 2026 — Bitbase today launched ORIGIN, the first season of its new Bitbase Points program. Ahead of the launch, the digital asset exchange credited points to eligible users who had been trading on the platform, so their past activity counts from day one. The season runs for 26 weeks, until May 4, 2027, with 1,000,000 points distributed each week.

ORIGIN is also the first part of Bitbase 2.0 to reach users directly. Bitbase unveiled 2.0 on November 2, with an upgraded app and website and a new brand identity built around the statement “Market Flows. We Focus.” The idea is that markets will always move, and Bitbase chooses to focus on what lasts for its users. ORIGIN applies the same thinking to participation. Rather than rewarding a single burst of activity, it looks at what users do day after day over six months and credits the contribution they make across that period.

Bitbase built ORIGIN around what users already do on the exchange. Eligible users, new or existing, are enrolled automatically, with no separate registration. Points are allocated daily based on each participant's contribution, which draws on four sources: trading, assets held on Bitbase, consistent activity and referrals. Because consistency is one of those sources, steady participation adds up over the course of the season.

ORIGIN also rewards users who bring others to Bitbase. A referrer receives an additional 25% of the contribution of each new user they refer directly, while the new user's own contribution is unaffected.

Starting November 9, participants will also receive a shareable Trading Identity card that reflects their trading habits, with a new card issued every Monday until the season ends.

"Bitbase 2.0 is about focus, and for our users, that means knowing their steady participation is recognized and credited," said Nicholas Lo, Chief Business Officer at Bitbase. "That's why ORIGIN started by crediting what users had already done with us. It doesn't ask anyone to trade differently. It simply records the participation that's already there, every day, for the next six months."

Users can track their points and rankings in the Bitbase app and on the website. Full details are available at bitbase.com/points.

Bitbase is a digital asset exchange serving individual and institutional users worldwide, with products spanning Spot, Futures, TradFi and Earn. Bitbase aims to give users a stable and straightforward trading experience, in line with its brand statement, “Market Flows. We Focus.” Learn more at bitbase.com.

#9586. Stock API Charts Need Complete Downloads and Explicit Data Gaps

Summary: A stock chart can look convincing even when its history is incomplete. A stock API supplies records under specific retrieval and aggregation rules; your application must finish the download and preserve missing observations. This article explains pagination, absent candles, and a small Python example that keeps an unknown price from becoming a false market move.

A stock API is a programmatic interface for retrieving stock-related data. For a historical chart, that often means requesting bars: records containing open, high, low, close, and volume for an interval. Those records can power chart viewers, research dashboards, and historical comparisons. They do not, by themselves, establish that every part of your requested window has been downloaded.

Consider a chart that has prices before and after a missing minute. Replacing the missing price with zero invents a collapse. Repeating the previous price creates a flat segment that was never observed. A sound implementation keeps the absence explicit while it determines whether the cause is normal market behavior, a retrieval problem, or a coverage limit.

The first completeness check belongs in the downloader. An HTTP success means a request succeeded; a paginated endpoint may still have more records to return.

Alpaca's Historical bars documentation gives a concrete example. Its multi-symbol results are ordered by symbol and then timestamp, so the first page can contain only one symbol. The page limit applies across the response, and a short page can still have a continuation token. An application must follow the documented token rather than decide that fewer rows means the download is finished.

That behavior is specific to the endpoint. Other APIs use different retrieval controls. TickDB's Candlestick Data endpoint, for example, exposes a symbol, interval, time bounds, and a record limit. Its documentation caps the limit at 1,000 and says the Free plan cannot specify start or end times. These constraints matter when designing a history browser: access to recent candles does not automatically provide arbitrary historical navigation.

Keep retrieval logic in the provider adapter. Confirm how boundaries and ordering work before splitting a request into time windows. If that behavior is undocumented, treat it as an unresolved integration requirement; guessing how to advance a timestamp can skip records or repeatedly retrieve the same window.

Figure 1. Suggested application flow. Retrieval follows the chosen endpoint's rules; validation and gap handling happen before rendering. This is a design illustration, not a measured system result.

Once retrieval has finished, a missing interval still needs interpretation. Databento's Aggregate bars documentation states that an interval without a trade produces no record. Under that convention, an absent bar can be an expected result. It does not establish that the service lost data, and the rule should not be assumed for every provider.

Start with the query context. Was the instrument trading during that period? Does the selected dataset cover the session you want? Does the provider omit intervals without qualifying observations? Did the downloader finish all required requests? These questions distinguish expected absence from an unexplained gap.

An exchange calendar also belongs in this interpretation. Do not generate a continuous minute grid across nights, weekends, and holidays and label every empty slot a failure. Use the calendar and session policy appropriate to the instrument. Keep timestamp conversion separate from session selection, including daylight saving changes.

Bar boundaries need their own check. Databento documents that its daily OHLCV schema follows UTC dates. A daily bucket therefore should not automatically be treated as the exchange-session day your chart intends to show.

Until the cause is established, a useful status is simply “no bar returned.” Labels such as “market closed” or “no trades” make stronger claims and need supporting context.

Suppose a synthetic series has a close of 100.00 at 14:30 UTC, no returned bar at 14:31, and a close of 101.00 at 14:32. The missing slot contains no observed close. It is neither a zero nor proof that the price stayed at 100.00.

For a close-price line, pass an explicit missing value to the chart adapter and configure the renderer to show a break. Some charting systems connect surrounding observations unless told otherwise, so inspect the rendered result as well as the input array. For candlesticks, do not manufacture an OHLC record from a missing slot.

Forward filling can serve a different purpose, such as displaying a last-known value in a dashboard. Preserve its original observation time and mark it as carried forward. Store that derived value separately from the observed series so it cannot silently become a reported trade or candle.

Figure 2. Synthetic close-price example in UTC. The middle slot has no returned observation. Its cause is unknown from these records alone; it must not become an invented zero-price candle.

The following Python example runs offline with synthetic data. It accepts an already selected, increasing UTC time grid and normalized close records for one instrument. It preserves missing slots, accepts identical duplicate records, and rejects conflicting duplicates instead of silently choosing a value.

The output is 14:30 100.00, 14:31 MISSING, and 14:32 101.00 on separate lines. The function has preserved what the input says without claiming why the middle slot is absent.

This is a close-series example, not a downloader or exchange calendar. Production adapters should use full normalized timestamps rather than time-of-day strings, partition records by instrument and series settings, and validate the complete OHLCV record. A conflicting revision may be legitimate, but resolving it requires a documented revision policy. Raising an error here makes that decision visible.

Open-source clients and data-processing tools can help build a stock API application. The distinction is between the software you can inspect or run and the underlying market-data service. An open-source client does not establish the upstream feed's coverage, usage rights, or historical depth.

For this charting task, inspect what the client does with pagination and missing values. A convenient wrapper may return a clean table while hiding a truncated query or a fill operation. Trace those transformations before using the result for research.

The same separation applies when using TickDB: the chart layer should retain the requested series settings and retrieval status alongside the returned candles. TickDB also documents that the final candle may still be forming. Mark that record as provisional when applicable; a changing current bar and an absent historical bar require different display behavior.

An acceptance check should cover more than whether the chart renders. Confirm that retrieval reached the endpoint's documented stopping condition, that the result is partitioned by the intended instrument and settings, and that unexplained gaps remain visible. Exercise an unfinished download, a missing slot, an identical duplicate, and a conflicting duplicate. Each should produce a deliberate result.

Do not turn the ratio of returned bars to clock minutes into a completeness score without establishing the expected-bar policy. A sparse instrument can legitimately have fewer bars under a trade-based aggregation rule. Conversely, a full-looking grid can conceal invented values.

The useful promise of a historical chart is that its displayed observations and limitations can be explained. A stock API supplies the records. The application must preserve the difference between a value that was observed, a value it derived, and a value it does not know.

Source basis: Alpaca Historical bars, Databento Aggregate bars, and TickDB Candlestick Data documentation, checked November 4, 2026. Code and numerical examples are synthetic.

#9585. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

In this article, we have taken a look at some of the biggest benefits associated with using sellfy for eCommerce. Once you compare these benefits to what you get with other platforms such as Shopify, you should find that it is worth your time to consider sellfy for your business. #9582. Flowise chatflows are public until an API key is attached

Flowise is used to build and run chatflows and agentflows. Its chatflow-level authorization documentation states the important default plainly: by default, a flow is available to the public, and anyone with the chatflow ID can run a prediction through the embed or API. Assigning an API key to that chatflow changes the API path so the caller must send the correct Authorization header.

On 2026-11-05, a count-only ZoomEye query with sub_type=all, page 1 and page size 1 returned 40,843 matches for app="Flowise". The title query returned 42,376. These counts do not show whether a given flow has an API key, what tools it can invoke or whether the instance has app-level authentication.

A chatflow can connect to models, vector stores, HTTP tools, credentials and document stores. An exposed prediction endpoint is therefore more than a chat UI. It can consume paid tokens, query private data or trigger tools. Inventory each flow's owner, public state, attached API key, credential references and downstream systems. Test an unauthenticated prediction request and record the exact response.

Assign a separate API key to each externally exposed flow where possible. Rotate the key when a widget is removed or a customer relationship ends. Treat the chatflow ID as discoverable metadata, not as a secret. If the ID appears in a public embed or support page, confirm that the flow's API key is still required.

Use network restrictions and rate limits around the Flowise instance. An app-level login protects the management UI, but the prediction route may be intentionally public. Restrict the server from reaching internal metadata, administrative networks and unapproved HTTP destinations. A flow that can fetch arbitrary URLs needs an egress policy independent of its chat prompt.

Store the Flowise encryption key separately from the deployment repository and back it up with the database. The documentation explains that it protects third-party credentials. If the key is regenerated or lost, existing credentials may fail to decrypt. A stolen key plus database access can expose the credentials attached to many flows.

Monitor for new public flows, API-key changes, bulk predictions and unusual tool calls. The ZoomEye result is a prioritization aid, not evidence of an exposed workflow. Use the exact application count to locate candidate instances, then verify the app authentication, flow settings and outbound tool access. The security boundary is the flow's executable authority, not just its chat input box.

#9578. Node.js Payment Reconciliation: Bounding Poison Retries Before Dead Letter Redrive

Consider this proposed page for an e-commerce service: the nightly payment reconciliation deadline has passed, and background job queue retries still haven't produced a completed settlement batch. The Node.js worker keeps returning the same poison message for another attempt. The on-call sees its business date, an increasing attempt count, and the same validation error. A green dashboard would be little comfort. What page fired, and why did the system wait until the deadline to distinguish a payment-provider interruption from input that another retry cannot repair?

TL;DR: Bound background job queue retries, send poison messages to a dead letter queue (DLQ), and record attempts and the last error outside the Node.js worker process. Standard queue delivery is at-least-once, so make reconciliation effects idempotent. Redrive only after correcting the cause, with a small, observable recovery batch. A queue receiving acknowledgments doesn't prove the payment ledger was reconciled.

This is a proposed incident analysis, not a report of a measured outage. Its decision axis is delivery guarantees: can a failed settlement batch remain visible without endlessly occupying the main queue, and can recovery repeat delivery without repeating its financial effects?

Start with the missing outcome. For this design, a logical reconciliation job identifies a merchant, provider, and settlement date; delivery receipts identify individual deliveries of that job. Those are different identities, and confusing them makes the incident harder to explain because a newly published message can look fresh while carrying the same permanently invalid settlement input. The operator needs to connect the current receipt to the logical job and its previous failures, including failures before a worker restart.

The earlier signal should expose an unresolved reconciliation approaching its deadline together with evidence that progress has stopped. Queue depth and DLQ growth belong beside that signal, since failed jobs can otherwise accumulate quietly, but neither metric establishes that the business operation completed. A falling queue can represent successful reconciliation or removal of work that still needs inspection. The completion record must settle that question.

For an illustrative policy, allow 4 processing attempts for a logical job before requiring inspection. Four is an application choice here, not a provider default or a universal recommendation. A permanent validation failure can go to inspection sooner; a transient provider error can consume the retry budget with exponential backoff. Select the budget against the nightly completion deadline and the provider's recovery behavior, rather than copying a count from an unrelated queue.

The trap is an endless negative-acknowledgment loop: the worker recognizes an error, returns the message for another delivery, and interprets that activity as recovery. A permanent error has no reason to improve between deliveries. If every attempt logs only a stack trace and loses its history on restart, the on-call can't tell whether the apparent first attempt is actually the hundredth.

Use the postmortem questions to define the control path before picking a product. Was the input valid? Did the provider fail temporarily? Was a financial effect committed before delivery was acknowledged? Which durable record answers each question? A failure classification should explain the next action, and an unknown error should still have a finite budget rather than a privileged route back into unlimited retries.

In the proposed reconciliation design, the durable application record contains the logical job identity, processing-attempt count, last error, completion state, and the input revision being processed. These are application fields, not claims about a queue response schema. Update them through the application's concurrency controls so two deliveries don't both believe they own the next attempt. Queue delivery counts remain useful evidence, but they cannot substitute for the business identity when a job is republished.

Acknowledge only when the required outcome is durably established. That includes recognizing that an earlier delivery already completed the same work. If the worker writes a reconciliation adjustment and dies before acknowledging delivery, its successor must recognize the existing adjustment rather than apply another one; a uniqueness constraint or equivalent transactional guard belongs around that business effect. An in-memory set disappears precisely when recovery needs it.

This creates a deliberate trade-off: durable bookkeeping adds application work, but it gives the responder evidence that survives delivery retries and process restarts. The queue handles delivery; the application must establish what completion means for the payment ledger. Don't claim exactly-once financial effects merely because a transport offers deduplication.

After a permanent failure, or after transient failures exhaust the budget, move the job out of the main processing flow into the DLQ for inspection. Preserve enough context to reproduce the error without treating a queue as the authoritative payment ledger. The important boundary is that the ordinary consumer stops treating the same unresolved failure as new work.

The instrumentation change is to record a processing decision with its reason, rather than logging only that a handler threw an exception. For every failed attempt, persist the logical job identity, input revision, attempt count, last error, and intended disposition: retry or inspection. Record completion separately. Keep the queue delivery identity as supporting evidence so the responder can trace repeated deliveries without mistaking them for separate settlement batches.

For the illustrative 4-attempt policy, the useful contrast is concrete: attempt 2 with a transient provider error means bounded retry remains possible; attempt 4 without completion means the job needs inspection. A permanent validation error at attempt 1 already calls for correction. Those decisions should be visible without opening a worker dashboard and guessing which spike corresponds to the merchant named in the page.

An event saying that inspection was requested isn't proof that the DLQ contains the message. Observe the resulting queue state as well. Otherwise the monitoring can celebrate a branch of code that never established the intended handoff. The same reasoning applies to redrive: requesting another delivery isn't evidence that reconciliation succeeded.

The following Go inspection utility can run beside a Node.js worker; it reads the DLQ without consuming or redriving it. Set INFRAI_ORIGIN to the service's HTTPS API origin, INFRAI_API_KEY to your key, and RECONCILIATION_QUEUE to the queue name. Save the block as main.go and run it with the Go toolchain. The retry budget here limits HTTP inspection attempts, independently of the reconciliation processing budget. It prints the response without inventing message fields; treat the output as potentially sensitive operational data.

Use Go 1.21 or later for this utility. It sends an explicit GET with bearer authentication, honors Retry-After within a bounded inspection deadline, and surfaces unsuccessful response bodies. It performs no writes, so it needs no write-idempotency key. It also doesn't implement the worker's financial idempotency guard; that belongs in the application's durable commit path.

A nightly reconciliation is an awkward place to confuse a scheduler, a work queue, a workflow engine, and a replayable event log. The fair comparison starts with the recovery operation the team needs, because a tool appropriate for retained event replay can impose unnecessary conceptual work on a bounded delivery task, while a simple delivery queue can leave a multi-step workflow's coordination inside application code.

These are real alternatives, but the table doesn't assert that they share one DLQ configuration, one attempt counter, or identical redrive behavior. Check the relevant product documentation before translating application policy into product settings. None removes the need to define a safe reconciliation effect.

Infrai fits the simple-queue case when the team also wants 295 routes across 20 modules under one key and one bill. That breadth shares one REST API, so adding another supported capability need not introduce another integration contract. No SDK is required for the inspection utility above; plain HTTP lets a Go incident tool inspect work delivered to a Node.js worker. Its self-describing API also exposes public discovery schemas without an API key, letting the team inspect declared request and response shapes before implementing delivery handling. The selection boundaries matter here. Standard queues are at-least-once, FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes, and acknowledged messages are deleted; retention is at most 30 days, payloads at most 256 KB, and delays at most 7 days. This isn't Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. There are no DAG or fan-out/join orchestration primitives, native debounce/throttle, or topic broadcast; broadcast requires separate queues. Cron execution is capped at 900 seconds, so longer reconciliation work needs cron to enqueue and a worker to consume. Cron targets must be public HTTP URLs, push targets public HTTPS; cron expressions exclude extensions such as L, paused triggers aren't backfilled, timing has second-level jitter, and run output retains only its first 4 KB. Keep durable reconciliation evidence in the application.

Those limits are decision criteria. If the payment workflow needs a dependency graph, retained event replay, or private push targets, evaluate the corresponding architecture before adopting the simple queue contract. If bounded delivery and inspection are sufficient, the narrower control model can be easier to explain during an incident.

Redrive follows a verified change: corrected settlement input, a fixed parser, or a resolved transient dependency failure. Preserve the original failure history and identify the corrected input revision. Grant a new, explicit recovery budget instead of resetting the old counter invisibly, because an operator must be able to distinguish a deliberate recovery attempt from a loop that merely acquired a new message identity.

Use one corrected logical job as the initial recovery batch in this proposed procedure. Confirm its durable reconciliation result, its acknowledgment, and the absence of duplicate financial effects before expanding the batch. If the same error recurs, stop the redrive and inspect the cause. Emptying the DLQ is a transport outcome; closing the incident requires accounting for the previously unresolved settlement work.

Finish the postmortem by reviewing the alert threshold. Paging on every DLQ arrival can turn each isolated bad input into an interruption even when inspection is already assigned and the nightly deadline remains safe; paging only on a large backlog can miss one merchant's reconciliation entirely. Neither extreme follows the business outcome. Separate routine inspection from urgent risk to completion, and tune against actual reconciliation deadlines and observed recovery behavior.

The cost of a threshold set too low is repeated interruption and eventually a page nobody trusts. Set it too high and the first useful signal arrives after the reconciliation window closes. Review what page fired, what action it enabled, and whether an earlier signal would have changed that action. A dashboard's color cannot answer those questions.

#9577. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.
