#9449. The Clothes That Make People Appear More Intelligent

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

How to use clothes to appear more competent.

Wearing more clothing makes you look more competent, a study finds.

Something as simple as taking off a sweater is enough to make you look less competent, the researchers found.

The finding applies to both men and women, said Dr Kurt Gray, the study’s first author:

“An important thing about our study is that, unlike much previous research, ours applies to both sexes.

It also calls into question the nature of objectification because people without clothes are not seen as mindless objects, but they are instead attributed a different kind of mind.”

The effect occurs because seeing more flesh encourages us to think about a person’s body, rather than their mind.

“We also show that this effect can happen even without the removal of clothes.

Simply focusing on someone’s attractiveness, in essence concentrating on their body rather than their mind, makes you see her or him as less of an agent [someone who acts and plans] more of an experiencer.”

Showing bare skin, though, does have some advantages, explained Dr Gray:

“A focus on the body, and the increased perception of sensitivity and emotion it elicits might be good for lovers in the bedroom.

Others appear to be less inclined to harm people with bare skin and more inclined to protect them.

In one experiment, for example, people viewing male subjects with their shirts off were less inclined to give those subjects uncomfortable electric shocks than when the men had their shirts on.”

“Even more than robbing someone of agency, the increased experience that may accompany body perceptions may lead those who are characterized in terms of their bodies to be seen as more reactive and emotional, traits that may also serve to work against career advancement.”

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Gray et al., 2011).

#9448. A Nasty Sign Of Omega-3 Deficiency

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

A high omega-3 diet can lower the signs and symptoms of the disease by 50 per cent.

Stiffness in the joints and swelling can be indirect signs of omega-3 deficiency, research suggests.

Waking up stiff in the morning, feeling pain in the joints, swelling, tenderness and loss of flexibility are all signs of arthritis.

Omega-3 deficiency could be contributing, as scientists believe there is a link between this leading cause of disability and a lack of omega-3 in the diet.

Researchers suggest that a diet rich in omega-3 could decrease the symptoms of osteoarthritis.

A study has found that adding fish oil to the diet — and to some degree flaxseed oil (alpha-linolenic acid has an anti-inflammatory effect) — can ease or even prevent osteoarthritis.

With population aging, osteoarthritis will be one of the leading causes of disability.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, by 2040 it is estimated that 26% of US adults aged 18 or older will be diagnosed by a doctor with arthritis.

While there are still no effective medications for treating this condition, omega-3 fish oil can be one of the best natural remedies in treating osteoarthritis.

Professor John Tarlton, the lead researcher of the study, explained the effect of omega-3 on osteoarthritis:

“Classic early signs of the condition, such as the degradation of collagen in cartilage and the loss of molecules that give it shock-absorbing properties, were both reduced with omega-3.

Furthermore, there was strong evidence that omega-3 influences the biochemistry of the disease, and therefore not only helps prevent disease, but also slows its progression, potentially controlling established osteoarthritis.”

Western diets contain high levels of omega-6 fatty acids, which can lead to inflammatory disorders such as colitis, heart disease, osteoporosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis.

Modern diets contain up to 30 times more omega-6 than omega-3, whereas our ancestor’s diets contained almost an equal level of these two omega fatty acids.

Therefore, supplementation with omega-3 can help to restore this imbalance in Western diets and improve conditions such as colitis and heart-related diseases.

Fish oil is much more effective than flax seed oil, but for vegetarians and vegans this supplement is an important option.

“Most diets in the developed world are lacking in omega-3, with modern diets having up to 30 times too much omega-6 and too little omega-3.

Taking omega-3 will help redress this imbalance and may positively contribute to a range of other health problems such as heart disease and colitis.”

The study was published in the journal of Osteoarthritis and Cartilage (Knott et al., 2011).

To air fry the chicken: Air fry at 375 for 10-12 minutes, or until at least 165 degrees internal temperature.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Oven): Toss 3-4 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt on a sheet pan. Roast the potatoes at 425 for 15 minutes. Scoot the potatoes over, add 3-4 cups broccoli and ¼ cup water to the same sheet pan, and roast for another 15 minutes.

Roasted Potatoes and Broccoli (Air Fryer): Toss 2 cups halved baby potatoes with avocado oil and salt. Air fry at 375 for 12 minutes. Add 2 cups frozen or fresh broccoli; air fry at 400 for another 10-12 minutes.

#9446. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

#9445. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

#9441. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#9439. Easy Jalapeño Corn Fritters (Vegan)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Just when we thought summer’s most perfect veggie couldn’t get any more delicious, corn FRITTERS graced our palettes. These crispy-on-the-outside, tender-on-the-inside, lightly spiced fritters are a must-try appetizer or side!

Not only are they incredibly delicious, but these fritters are vegan, optionally gluten-free, and SO easy to make! Grab your mixing bowl and 10 basic ingredients, and you’ll be enjoying fritters in 30 minutes or less. What are you waiting for? Let’s do this, friends!

Giving traditional corn fritters a vegan spin requires a couple adjustments. First, instead of eggs for binding, we rely on flaxseed meal. And instead of milk, we rely on a neutral-flavored, unsweetened dairy-free milk (homemade cashew being our favorite). The rest of the ingredients are pretty classic, but we gave these fritters our own flavor spin and also made them gluten-free!

Besides flaxseed meal and dairy-free milk, the ingredients for the batter include baking powder for fluffiness; salt, garlic powder, and nutritional yeast for flavor; and all-purpose flour or gluten-free blend to thicken it.

You’re looking for a thick, fluffy batter, which can be achieved by adding more flour or dairy-free milk as needed. With the batter ready, we’re just 3 ingredients away from fritter time!

Next up, fresh corn gets nestled into the chunky batter, along with finely chopped jalapeño for a subtle heat. While we love using fresh ingredients when it’s summertime, this recipe also works with frozen corn — just let it thaw at room temperature, then pat dry with paper towels to remove extra moisture. And if you don’t have fresh jalapeño, a pinch of cayenne would likely work as well!

Now for the frying! Instead of deep frying, we go with a shallow fry, cooking for 2-3 minutes per side in avocado oil in a cast iron skillet. Not only do we find shallow frying less daunting, but it minimizes the amount of oil needed and maximizes the health benefits. Win, win, win! And still, major YUM!

When the fritters are golden on both sides, it’s time to enjoy! They’re incredibly flavorful on their own (we were snacking right off the cooling rack), but they’re also amazing paired with a sauce. Try our Go-To Guacamole, Creamy Cashew Jalapeño Sauce, or Easy Vegan Ranch Dressing.

We hope you LOVE these corn fritters, friends! They’re:SavoryCrispyNaturally a little sweetJust a little spicyQuick & easy& SO delicious!

This is the perfect appetizer or side to make during peak summer, when fresh corn and jalapeños are in season! However, they’re so delicious you may find yourself craving them year-round (in which case, using frozen corn is also a great option).

These fritters are flavorful without being heavily seasoned, making them a good fit for pairing with a variety of other sides and mains, especially grilled proteins, side salads, and anything BBQ seasoned (hello, summertime!). Here are several delicious pairings:

#9436. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

#9434. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9433. The Elephant in the Rheum – “Burnout” Among the Workforce

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

This article originally appeared on Rheumatology Advisor

This can happen with baked goods that only use oats. Did you let the batter sit out for a while? Baking the batter right away can sometimes help.

As expected given all your other great recipes, these were DELICIOUS and the whole family loved them! My intention was to freeze some but I don’t think they will last that long at my house. Will definitely make again!

My vitamix didn’t do a great job blending when I started with oats at the bottom. I’ll add the liquid ingredients first next time.

oh, that’s a good note – for the liquids to go first!

Just ordered the FULLSTAR chopper! Thanks for the recommendation. So much faster to get dinner ready. Smooch!~!

Easy and delicious! I made them with my toddler and we gobbled them up. I lowered the sugar to 1/2c and baked the extra batter into mini muffins that cooked in 12 minutes 🙂

These are SO GOOD and soooo nice and easy cause of blending everything. I used coconut sugar instead of brown, and gala apples instead of honeycrisp cause it’s what I had on hand, and they turned out amazing. Definitely going on the repeat list!

Thank you for yet another amazing POY recipe!! Absolutely delicious!Followed the recipe almost exactly, except I had to sub 0% Greek Yogurt for the whole milk version as that’s all I have. I ate two in a row straight out of the oven, so yummy. Can’t wait to have one with my coffee in the morning and the rest will go in the freezer for a perfect breakfast-on-the-go for my daughter who has an hour bus ride to college very early. I’ve made so many POY recipes now (made the Apple Crisp for dessert today too) they never fail, are always delicious and the whole family (fussy husband, two teens, a tween…and occasionally a 5yr old Labrador) love them.

I don’t have a Vitamix but this definitely didn’t work in my super basic blender! I ended up using my food processor with the oats first, then adding everything after. That worked great!

Oh, thank you for the notes on using the food processor! I know others were interested in using it.

Delightful little fall recipe! Not too sweet, was great w my coffee this morning. I used what apples I had on hand (gala)= 2.5 small ones. My cupcake pan holds 12, so I used my mini pan w/ the extra batter and got 16 minis too. (Cooked those for about 12 minutes along with the big ones).

I would make these again. It was a little putzsy as I only have a mini blender, so I had to blend in batches.

I swapped the oats for oat flour I already had and didn’t check my ratio so it made a few more muffins (3.5 cups oats = roughly 2.67 cups oat flour). Also added about .5 cup of oats to the topping to get an apple crisp topping.

Would love to know why you don’t recommend the Costco sprouted oats, that’s almost all we use. Love all your recipes and look forward to trying this!

Lauren, I just wanted to let you know my family made these with the Costco sprouted oats because that’s what we had on hand and we were impatient. My family still loved them and they were worth making. I’m guessing they would have been a little softer with old-fashioned rolled oats because they were maybe slightly tough, BUT it really wasn’t an issue for us.

I have applesauce on hand instead of fresh apples, would that work as a substitute?

Also curious about applesauce, if it’s getting blended already!

These are delicious! I didn’t have a full cup of Greek yogurt so I added some cottage cheese and sour cream to make 1 cup. Otherwise followed the recipe as written. Supper easy to make and everyone loved them. Will definitely make these again.

These look delicious! Can you use sour cream instead of greek yoghurt?

Could you use food processor instead of blender? Excited to try this!

I used a food processor and they came out great!

These sound delicious. You mentioned that you used brown sugar instead of maple syrup for this recipe. If I preferred to use maple syrup, what would be the recommended amount?

I haven’t tried it – I just went straight for the brown sugar to save some dollars. 🙂 And the flavor is delicious. But I would like to try it, just so we know how it works with maple syrup. I will report back when I do! (I have several muffins in this same style and they use between 1/2 cup and 3/4 cup maple syrup, but I don’t want to confirm that for this one until I know for sure.)

Lindsay said in the article that the Costco sprouted oats aren’t recommended because they absorb liquid a different way. She also said quick oats do as well and that’s why they’re not recommended either.

#9431. Spiced Cranberry Cherry Cobbler

Spiced Cranberry Cherry Cobbler

This spiced cranberry cherry cobbler combines sweet cherries and tart cranberries with a warmly spiced buttery biscuit topping. Orange zest, cinnamon, and nutmeg add cozy flavor, while a little brown sugar gives the tender biscuits a hint of sweetness. The fruit filling thickens as it bakes, bubbling up around the golden fluffy topping. Serve it warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream for a comforting dessert that's especially welcome during the fall and winter months.

#9430. 1-Bowl Honey Almond Snack Cake (Gluten-Free)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

Honey almond snack cake!? You know you want to jump in on the fun! This GORGEOUS loaf is perfectly moist with a lightly floral flavor and beautiful sponge texture. Bonus? It’s made without gluten or dairy, but no one will know.

It’s the perfect cake for afternoon tea, brunch gatherings, and beyond! Just 10 ingredients, 1 bowl, and simple methods (no mixer) required. Let’s bake!

This light, fluffy gluten-free honey almond cake is made with 10 simple ingredients:

After mixing together your wet ingredients, then adding your dry ingredients, it’s time to pour the batter into a parchment-lined loaf pan. The parchment paper will prevent sticking and make it super easy to remove the cake from the pan.

We also think this cake would work beautifully in an 8-inch round cake pan, but it will bake much faster!

Top with sliced almonds before baking, then pop that beauty in the oven! After baking and letting the cake cool slightly, we love to add an extra drizzle of honey. Deliciousness awaits, friends!

We hope you LOVE this honey almond cake! It’s:FluffyFloralSpongySubtly sweetPerfectly moist& SO delicious!

Grab a slice of cake, pour yourself a mug of coffee or tea, kick back, and get your snack on! It would also pair well with Earl Grey Tea, our Lemon Ginger Jasmine Iced Tea, or a Cinnamon Vanilla Dandelion Tea Latte.

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

Have a question? Use ctrl+f or ⌘+f on your computer or the "find on page" function on your phone browser to search existing comments! Need help? Check out this tutorial!

Can this be made without honey? If so, what would be the substitute?

Hi Jessica, perhaps agave or maple syrup, but we haven’t tested with those alternatives. The flavor will vary, especially if using maple. Let us know if you try it out!

wow – I absolutely loved this! Incredible flavor and very tender crumb… I can’t believe this combo of pantry ingredients could produce such a fantastic GF cake. And full disclosure – I was kind of winging it with what I had, so I made a version of GF flour with potato starch, white rice flour, sourgum flour and oat flour, and I only had whole almonds so I chopped them roughly for the top. I baked it in my air fryer – a total experiment, and I had to cover it with foil after 10 minutes (did it in an 8×8 pan) – and while it didn’t come out perfectly (it cooked a little unevenly), it was utterly delicious! So moist, with the browned sides and beautifully browned almonds (a benefit of the air fryer, maybe). All to say – this recipe is very adaptable and honestly so so scrumptious. I just had to tell you!

We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Ann! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo

Could I use almond meal instead of almond flour? Or would the change in texture be too drastic?

Hey Serena! We think it would work, but the flavor and texture might change a bit! Let us know if you try it!

Honey almond snack cake looks like the perfect simple bake. Appreciate how approachable the steps stay while still feeling special — trying a small cake for weekend coffee.

I made this as written (but with butter) and it is delightful! I love everything about it! Thanks for another great recipe!

We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Lisa! Thanks so much for the lovely review. xo

Made this and loooove it! Came out really fluffy and delicious. Only modification is brand – I used Earth balance plant butter and Silk protein vegan vanilla yogurt. I also baked slightly longer as the core was still really wet at 45 minutes. Ended up being closer to 55-57mins in my oven. Great recipe, thanks!

We’re so glad you enjoyed it, Teya! Thanks so much for sharing. xo

I made this and it came out delicious. I was wondering if I could 1/2 cup of applesauce for added moisture?

We’re so glad you enjoyed it! Applesauce might make it a bit too dense, but let us know if you do any experimenting!

I followed the recipe and I added 1/2 cup unsweetened applesauce. It added a nice flavor (apples go well with honey) and it made it moist. It was a tiny bit more dense, but it helped to maintain the texture throughout the week.

We’re so glad you enjoyed it with the applesauce, Susan! Thanks so much for sharing. xo

I made this today with flax egg and it came out beautifully.

Some specifics: My flax egg was made with aquafaba instead of water (I had some handy from a fresh pot of chickpeas). My flour was a GF flour from my local grocery store’s private label. I baked it in an 8″ round glass cake pan in my toaster oven. My crumb was tender but a little more dense than yours (and darker due to the flax and my blend of flour).

We’re so glad the flax egg worked, Sara! Thanks so much for the lovely review and for sharing your modifications. xo

Hi! Where do you manage to find Miyoko’s vegan butter? We live in Florida and sadly I haven’t been able to find it at our Whole Foods for almost a year already!! So sad as it has no replacement! Also – I love honey in cakes but stopped using it as heated honey is unhealthy. Would maple work here if I can get the butter?

Hey there! Sprouts usually has Miyoko’s if Whole Food’s doesn’t. You could also use another vegan butter here. We have learned that heated honey isn’t necessarily unhealthy, heating it just get’s rid of some of the benefits of raw honey. It’s still safe to bake with! We’re not sure if maple syrup would work, but let us know if you try it!

Sounds like another great recipe! Do you think I make it in muffin tins instead? How long would the bake time be then? Thank you! /Mattis

Hey Mattis! We haven’t tried the recipe as muffins, but we think it would definitely work! We would suggest starting with a 23 minute bake time and then checking them every 3-5 minutes after until done! Let us know if you try it.

This recipe is perfect for Rosh Hashanah shana! I can’t wait to make it for the high holidays. Do you think that I could add chunks of apple or decorate it with sliced apples on top?

We’re so glad, Caryn! We’re not sure exactly how the cake would react to the apple, but our suggestion would be if you do add chunks to the cake to coat them in a little flour first to make sure they don’t sink to the bottom! Then you can fold the flour coated apples into the cake right before you add the batter to the pan. They might work on top of the cake, but we would suggest watching it while it bakes to make sure they don’t burn! Let us know if you try it either way!

I think I’m going to try subbing sourdough starter for yogurt–I’ll report back with results!

#9429. Chocolate Caramel Pecan Tart

Chocolate Caramel Pecan Tart

This chocolate caramel pecan tart combines a buttery chocolate pastry crust with a rich, chewy chocolate caramel filling and plenty of toasted pecans. Every slice delivers the perfect mix of chocolate, caramel, and nutty crunch, and a sprinkle of flaky sea salt on top brings it all together. Cook the filling on the stovetop, then let the refrigerator do the rest. This is a wonderful make-ahead dessert!
